config.title: Request Deduplication

intro.title: Request Deduplication
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple Vue application that demonstrates request deduplication, a technique to prevent sending the same network request multiple times. You will learn how to use a JavaScript Map to track ongoing requests and ensure duplicate calls are avoided. The core concept involves checking if a request is already in progress before initiating a new one, improving performance and reducing server load. You will implement this using Vue's reactive state and computed properties to manage request statuses. By the end, you'll have a functional app that fetches data efficiently without redundant API calls.
intro.usecase: Request deduplication is essential in modern web applications where multiple components might trigger the same API call simultaneously. In a Vue dashboard displaying real-time analytics, multiple widgets could request the same user data, causing unnecessary network traffic. This pattern prevents duplicate requests when users rapidly click search buttons or apply filters in data tables. It's also crucial in e-commerce product listings where sorting and filtering actions shouldn't trigger redundant API calls for the same product data.

objectives: Implement a Vue composable function to track in-flight requests
Apply request deduplication logic to prevent duplicate API calls
Construct a reactive state object to manage pending request status
Configure computed properties to determine if a request is already in progress
Integrate the deduplication mechanism with existing API service calls
Manipulate the request tracking state when requests start and complete
Render UI feedback based on the deduplication status

steps.title: Import Vue and ref from vue
steps.instruction: Import Vue and ref from the 'vue' package to use reactive references in your component.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in the necessary Vue APIs. This is the foundation for reactive state management.
steps.analogousExample:
// Importing core Vue APIs
import { ref, reactive } from 'vue'
steps.expectedOutcome: The Vue and ref APIs are imported and ready to use for reactive state management.
successCriteria: Vue and ref are imported from the 'vue' package.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.

steps.feedbackWrong: Check your import statement. You need to import both Vue and ref from the 'vue' package.

steps.hint: In Vue, you can create a component by defining a template and script section. The template should have a single root element, typically a <div>.
steps.expectedOutcome: A Vue component named 'RequestDeduplication' is created with a template containing a root <div> element and a script section.

steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure the component is named 'RequestDeduplication' and has both template and script sections.

steps.hint: Use the ref function you imported earlier to create reactive state. Initialize it with an empty string value.
steps.analogousExample:

const inputValue = ref('');
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a reactive state variable called 'responseData' initialized with an empty string, ready to store API responses.
successCriteria: The component contains a ref called 'responseData' initialized with an empty string value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're using the ref function and initializing it with an empty string.

steps.title: Initialize reactive state for loading status
steps.instruction: Inside the setup function, create a ref named isLoading to track whether a request is currently loading. Initialize it with false.

steps.analogousExample:
// Example: creating a reactive loading state
const isLoading = ref(false);
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a reactive isLoading state initialized to false, ready to track loading status.
successCriteria: A ref named isLoading is created inside setup() and initialized with false.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you're creating a ref named 'isLoading' and initializing it with false inside the setup function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The loading state wasn't properly initialized. Remember to use ref() to create a reactive reference named 'isLoading' with an initial value of false.

steps.title: Create a map to track pending requests
steps.instruction: Inside the setup function, create a JavaScript Map object to store pending request promises. Name it 'pendingRequests'.
steps.hint: Initialize a new Map using 'const pendingRequests = new Map();' within the setup function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: creating a Map to track items
const itemMap = new Map();
steps.expectedOutcome: A Map object named 'pendingRequests' is created inside the setup function to track pending request promises.
successCriteria: The 'pendingRequests' Map is declared within the setup function.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you've created a Map named 'pendingRequests' inside the setup function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The Map for tracking pending requests is missing or incorrectly placed. Create a Map named 'pendingRequests' inside the setup function.

steps.title: Define the fetchData function
steps.instruction: Inside the setup function, define an async function named fetchData that takes a url parameter and makes a fetch request to that URL.
steps.hint: Use the async keyword before function and await with fetch. The function should return the fetch promise.
steps.expectedOutcome: The fetchData function is defined and ready to be used for making API requests.
successCriteria: An async function named fetchData is defined inside setup, takes a url parameter, and uses fetch to make a request.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure fetchData is an async function that takes a url parameter and uses fetch.
steps.feedbackWrong: The fetchData function is not properly defined. It should be async, take a url parameter, and use fetch.

steps.title: Implement request deduplication logic
steps.instruction: Inside the fetchData function, add logic to check if a request for the same URL is already pending in the pendingRequests map before making a new fetch call.
steps.hint: Use the pendingRequests map to store and retrieve fetch promises. If a promise for the given URL already exists, return that promise instead of creating a new one.
steps.expectedOutcome: The fetchData function will now check the pendingRequests map before making a new fetch, preventing duplicate requests for the same URL.
successCriteria: The fetchData function includes a check for existing promises in pendingRequests and returns the existing promise if found.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure to check the pendingRequests map and return the existing promise when a request for the same URL is already in progress.
steps.feedbackWrong: The deduplication logic is missing. Remember to check if the URL already exists in pendingRequests before making a new fetch call.
